title: Looped network vs OWA-EPANET 2.2
description: A five-pipe looped network solved by both engines from identical inputs. All five pipe flows agree with OWA-EPANET 2.2 to within about 0.003% - independent-engine agreement, the strongest check we run.

title: Three-reservoir junction (Darcy-Weisbach)
description: The classic textbook problem: three reservoirs at 40, 28 and 15 m feed a common junction, and the middle reservoir correctly receives flow. Verifies the junction mass balance and the flow-direction signs.

title: Single pipe, turbulent (vs Colebrook-White)
description: FNS uses the explicit Churchill (1977) correlation, which agrees with Colebrook-White in the turbulent range to a fraction of a percent.

title: Laminar line (Hagen-Poiseuille, exact)
description: Churchill reduces exactly to the laminar f = 64/Re below Re = 2000, matching the analytic solution.

title: Fully rough pipe (von Karman limit)
reference_class: Published limiting correlation (von Karman fully rough limit)
description: 500 m of DN300 at 3 mm roughness under 20 m of head. At eps/D = 0.01 and Re ~ 1.9 million the flow is deep in the fully rough regime, where friction stops depending on the Reynolds number. The solver's Churchill correlation lands 0.16% off the roughness-only limit, which is the expected residual, not agreement by construction.

title: Pump + system operating point
description: A pump feeding two parallel branches. The solver finds the operating point where the fitted pump curve (here exactly H = 25 - 8000 Q^2) meets the system curve.

title: Variable-speed pump at 85% (affinity laws)
description: The same pump and twin branches as the duty-point case, run at 85% speed. Head and flow scale by the affinity laws (H with s squared, Q with s) and the solve finds the new operating point on the scaled curve against the two-branch system resistance.

title: Single pipe, Hazen-Williams (closed form)
description: hf = 10.674 L Q^1.852 / (C^1.852 D^4.871), C = 130. The solver, the closed form and EPANET's native Hazen-Williams all use this constant.

title: Three-reservoir junction, Hazen-Williams
description: Three reservoirs (100, 80, 40 m) to a common junction. Verifies the junction mass balance and flow-direction signs under Hazen-Williams.

title: Isothermal gas pipeline pressure drop
description: Air from 600 to 400 kPa absolute down a 200 m line: a 33% density fall. The gas kernel solves in pressure-squared with the exact isothermal relation. Density falls and velocity climbs toward the outlet.

title: Methane trunk line, delivery pressure
description: 2.5 kg/s of methane down 5 km of DN150 from 3000 kPa absolute. This is the inverse problem an operator actually asks: fix the throughput and find the pressure you arrive with. Solved in pressure-squared form at Re = 1.9 million.

title: Insulated hot-water main, delivered temperature
description: A 70 °C main, 200 m of DN100 with 30 mm of insulation, ambient 15 °C. The coupled thermal-hydraulic solve builds the per-metre U from an inner film, the steel wall and the lagging.

title: Hot line cooling along its length (exact)
description: 1.5 kg/s of water entering 250 m of line at 80 °C, ambient 10 °C, at a fixed 2.5 W/(m·K). The analytic solution of the steady one-dimensional energy balance, which the coupled thermal-hydraulic solve reproduces to the last figure shown.

title: Mixing junction, blended temperature (exact)
description: 2 kg/s at 90 °C meeting 3 kg/s at 30 °C. Temperature does not average, energy does: the mix leaves at 54 °C, not 60 °C. The network carries the blend downstream on the same balance.

title: Three-reservoir junction, power-law fluid
description: A shear-thinning power-law fluid (K = 0.5, n = 0.5) in a three-reservoir junction. Each pipe picks its regime from the generalised Reynolds number. Two run turbulent and one laminar.

title: Laminar power-law line (exact)
description: A shear-thinning fluid (K = 2.5, n = 0.45) at 1 L/s down 50 m of DN50, generalised Reynolds number 103, so firmly laminar. The analytic power-law solution exists here and the solver matches it exactly.

title: Laminar Bingham line (Buckingham-Reiner)
description: A yield-stress sludge (8 Pa, plastic viscosity 0.03 Pa·s) at 2 L/s down 100 m of DN80. The core travels as an unsheared plug, which is what the Buckingham-Reiner relation accounts for and a Newtonian friction estimate cannot.

title: Turbulent power-law line (Dodge-Metzner)
description: The same rheology pushed into turbulence: 14 L/s down 200 m of DN80 at a generalised Reynolds number of 7762. The implicit Dodge-Metzner relation is solved here from its published form and compared with what the solver produces.

title: Turbulent Bingham line (Darby-Melson)
description: A yield-stress fluid at 3 m/s in DN100: Bingham Reynolds number 33 000 against a Hedstrom number of 440 000. The Hanks criterion puts this above the transition, so the turbulent Darby-Melson friction applies rather than the plug-flow relation.

title: Single pipe, fixed friction factor (closed form)
description: hf = f (L/D) V^2/2g, f = 0.02. Reproduces textbook examples stated at a fixed friction factor.

title: Active PRV regulating a line
description: A PRV set to 60 m on a 100 m to 30 m line goes ACTIVE and pins its downstream head to 60.0000 m exactly - the Studio solves the setting to identity. The regulated flow is then fixed by the downstream leg alone. It matches the closed-form value and OWA-EPANET 2.2, in the same global-gradient family.

title: FCV clamping the flow to a setpoint
description: An FCV set to 170 L/s holds the through-flow to its setpoint exactly. The head it must destroy (45.0 m) and the resulting upstream head match the closed-form value and OWA-EPANET 2.2.

title: Check valve blocking reverse flow
description: Forward, a non-return check valve passes flow as a plain K = 2.5 fitting (bit-identical). On a reverse gradient it shuts and carries exactly zero, where a loss-only fitting would pass 282 L/s backwards - the reverse-flow defect this element closes. Both legs agree with OWA-EPANET 2.2.

title: GFSSP Example 1: pump, valve and pipe
description: A pump feeding a receiving reservoir through a gate valve and 1500 ft of pipe. FNS solves 189.6 lb/s against GFSSP's 191 lb/s - independent codes (GFSSP is a finite-volume solver, not a global-gradient one) agreeing to under a percent.

title: GFSSP Example 2: distribution network, main branch
description: A 10-pipe distribution network with four fixed-pressure boundaries. The inlet branch carries about 100 lb/s, and all ten branch flows agree with GFSSP within 3%, including two that run in reverse.

title: GFSSP Example 2: a reverse-flowing branch
description: Branch 6 to 8 carries flow in reverse (a negative from-to flow). The signed result reproduces GFSSP's direction and magnitude - a genuine test of the network's flow-direction bookkeeping.

title: GFSSP Example 22: fixed-flow boundary
description: A +100 and -10 lb/s pair of fixed-flow boundaries leaves a net 90 lb/s carried by the branch, fixed by conservation. FNS reproduces it exactly, matching GFSSP.

title: Thin sharp-edged orifice, loss coefficient
description: For a diameter ratio beta = 0.5, the Studio's sharp-orifice correlation gives K = 29.7, within 3% of GFSSP's turbulent option-5 value of 30.49. Referenced to the upstream velocity head, as GFSSP does.

title: Sudden expansion (Borda-Carnot)
description: The Studio uses the exact Borda-Carnot result K = (1 - beta^2)^2 = 0.5625 at beta = 0.5, within 2% of GFSSP's turbulent option-8 value of 0.5715.

title: Sudden contraction, loss coefficient
description: The Studio evaluates the GFSSP option-7 turbulent contraction formula on the upstream velocity head. At beta = 0.5 it reproduces the published K = 7.32 to better than 0.1%.

title: Non-circular duct via hydraulic diameter
description: A 200 x 100 mm rectangular duct carrying 50 L/s of water: the Darcy-Weisbach / Churchill pipe model runs on the hydraulic diameter D_h = 4A/P = 0.1333 m and the true flow area, giving hf = 0.410 m within 0.5% of a closed-form calculation on the same hydraulic diameter.
